tool-phone-laptop-devmode.title: Connect your phone to a laptop with Developer Mode (Android + iOS)
tool-phone-laptop-devmode.note: Turn on Developer options, install adb, connect by cable and wirelessly, control the screen with scrcpy; iPhone: Developer Mode, Xcode, Safari Web Inspector, libimobiledevice. All commands included.

sections.t: Android can do almost everything through adb (install apps, copy files, view the screen, run commands). Apple locks the iPhone down much more: mostly logs, screen recording/mirroring and web debugging. This guide covers each system separately.
Only turn on Developer Mode / USB debugging on your own phone and only trust your own laptop. This permission gives the laptop deep control over the phone; don't use public computers.
PART 1 · ANDROID
Step 1: Turn on Developer options

items.d: Samsung: About phone → Software information. Some phones: Settings → About phone.
The phone shows “You are now a developer”. Enter your PIN/password if asked.
Usually under Settings → System → Developer options (Samsung: at the bottom of the main Settings page).
Xiaomi/Redmi: also turn on “Install via USB” and “USB debugging (Security settings)” if you want to control it with a mouse.

sections.t: Step 2: Install adb on the laptop
adb comes with Google's SDK Platform-Tools, free.

# Windows: download the zip at developer.android.com/tools/releases/platform-tools, unzip it,
# open PowerShell in that folder and type  .\adb version

# macOS
brew install --cask android-platform-tools

# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt install adb

# Check
adb version
Step 3: Plug in the cable and allow access

items.t: Use a USB cable that transfers data
items.d: A charge-only cable won't be detected. If the phone asks for a USB mode, choose “File transfer”.

items.t: Tap “Allow USB debugging” on the phone
items.d: Tick “Always allow from this computer” and tap Allow.
Type adb devices. A status of device means it worked.

sections.t: adb devices -l

items: unauthorized: you haven't tapped Allow on the phone. Unplug and replug the cable, or run adb kill-server then adb devices.
Device not found: try another cable/port and check that USB debugging is on. Windows may need the manufacturer's USB driver (Samsung, Xiaomi…).
Linux says “no permissions”: set up a udev rule for your phone brand, or rerun adb with the right permissions.

sections.t: Step 4: Common adb commands

# Install / uninstall apps
adb install app.apk
adb install -r app.apk          # reinstall, keep data
adb uninstall com.ten.goi

# Copy files
adb push file.txt /sdcard/Download/
adb pull /sdcard/DCIM/Camera/ ./anh

# Take a screenshot
adb shell screencap -p /sdcard/s.png
adb pull /sdcard/s.png

# Record the screen (max 3 minutes by default, Ctrl+C to stop)
adb shell screenrecord /sdcard/demo.mp4
adb pull /sdcard/demo.mp4

# Open a shell on the phone / view logs
adb shell
adb logcat

# List installed apps
adb shell pm list packages

# Type and tap remotely
adb shell input text hello
adb shell input tap 540 1200
adb shell input keyevent 4      # 4=Back, 3=Home, 26=Power

# Reboot
adb reboot

# When adb hangs
adb kill-server
adb start-server
Step 5: Connect wirelessly (Android 11 and later)
The phone and laptop must be on the same Wi-Fi network. You only need to pair once per laptop.

items.d: Developer options → Wireless debugging → on.
Tap “Pair device with pairing code”. The phone shows a pairing IP:port and a 6-digit code.

items.t: Run the pair command on the laptop
items.d: Type adb pair IP:PAIRING-PORT and enter the 6-digit code.
The main Wireless debugging screen shows a different IP:port (the connection port). Type adb connect IP:CONNECT-PORT. This port may change each time you turn it back on.

sections.t:
adb pair 192.168.1.20:37099
# enter the 6-digit code when asked
adb connect 192.168.1.20:41555
adb devices

# Disconnect
adb disconnect
sections.cap: Example (replace with the IP and ports on your phone)

sections.t: Android 10 and earlier: plug in the cable once, type adb tcpip 5555, unplug, then adb connect phone-IP:5555.
Step 6: View and control the phone screen on the laptop (scrcpy)
scrcpy is an open-source tool. It needs no app on the phone and uses the same adb connection above (cable or wireless). You can control the phone with your mouse and keyboard.

# Windows (if you have winget) or download the zip from the GitHub page (adb included)
winget install --exact Genymobile.scrcpy

# macOS
brew install scrcpy

# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt install scrcpy

# Run (phone has USB debugging on and is connected)
scrcpy

# Common options
scrcpy --turn-screen-off --stay-awake     # turn off the phone screen, keep it awake
scrcpy --max-size 1024                    # lower the resolution for smoother playback
scrcpy --record demo.mp4                  # watch and record at the same time
scrcpy -s SERIAL                          # pick a device when several are connected
Install commands and option names may differ depending on your scrcpy version and OS. Check the scrcpy README on GitHub for the latest commands.
Turn it off when not in use

items: Turn off USB debugging and Wireless debugging when you're done.
Developer options → “Revoke USB debugging authorizations” to remove trusted laptops.

sections.t: PART 2 · iPHONE (iOS)

Know this first: iPhone has no adb. Apple doesn't let a laptop control the screen remotely like Android. What you can do: view logs, record/mirror the screen, debug web pages in Safari, install dev apps with Xcode (Mac).
Step 1: Trust the computer

items.t: Plug the iPhone into the laptop with a cable
items.d: Use a Lightning/USB-C cable that transfers data.
Enter your passcode when asked. On Windows, also install the Apple Devices app (or iTunes) for the driver, otherwise the phone won't be detected.

sections.t: Step 2: Turn on Developer Mode (iOS 16 and later)

items.d: Scroll to the bottom and find “Developer Mode”.
The iPhone will ask to restart.
Unlock the phone, tap “Turn On” and enter your passcode.

sections.t: The Developer Mode option may not appear until the iPhone has been connected to Xcode on a Mac or has a dev build of an app installed. This is how iOS works, not a problem with your phone.
Step 3A: If you have a Mac

items.d: Open Xcode → Window → Devices and Simulators. Tick “Connect via network” to connect wirelessly after pairing by cable.
Open QuickTime Player → File → New Movie Recording, click the arrow next to the record button and choose the iPhone as the source.

iPhone: Settings → Safari → Advanced → turn on Web Inspector (on newer iOS it may be under Settings → Apps → Safari). Mac: Safari → Settings → Advanced → turn on “Show features for web developers”. Open the page on the iPhone, then go to the Develop menu on the Mac and choose the iPhone's name and the page to inspect.

sections.t: Step 3B: If you use Windows or Linux
The open-source libimobiledevice toolkit can read device info and logs. Some commands (like screenshots) depend on the iOS version: iOS 17 and later need a different tool, e.g. pymobiledevice3.

# macOS (Homebrew)
brew install libimobiledevice

# Ubuntu / Debian
sudo apt install libimobiledevice-utils usbmuxd

# Pair and check
idevicepair pair
idevice_id -l                 # list UDIDs
ideviceinfo                   # device info
idevicesyslog                 # live logs
idevicescreenshot shot.png    # may not work on iOS 17+

# iOS 17+: pymobiledevice3 (requires Python)
pip install pymobiledevice3
pymobiledevice3 usbmux list
pymobiledevice3 syslog live
Some pymobiledevice3 commands on iOS 17+ need a “tunnel” running and admin rights. See the project's docs on GitHub for the syntax for your version.
Mirror the iPhone screen to a laptop without a cable

items: Mac: use Control Center on the iPhone → Screen Mirroring, or QuickTime with a cable as above.
Windows: Windows can't receive AirPlay out of the box. You need a third-party AirPlay receiver app. Check its reliability and price yourself before using it.
This guide hasn't tested each third-party app individually.

sections.t: Security notes for both systems

items: Turn off Developer Mode (iPhone) or USB debugging (Android) when not in use.
Don't plug into public charging stations while debugging is on. If a “Trust / Allow” dialog pops up unexpectedly, tap Don't Trust / Deny.
Don't run unfamiliar adb or pip commands copied from unknown sources. Many commands can delete data.

buy-ovh-hermes.title: OVH VPS for Hermes Agent: picking a plan and a setup checklist
buy-ovh-hermes.note: Compares OVH VPS-1 to VPS-5, Hermes Agent's requirements, which plan I'd pick, and a checklist for setting it up on a VPS.

sections.t: How to read this: plan specs and prices come from search results (the OVH US page and comparison sites). I couldn't open the OVHcloud page itself, so they aren't confirmed at the source. Sources disagree on VPS-4 and VPS-5. Check the OVHcloud VPS page before buying. The 'my pick' section is opinion.
1. OVH VPS plans compared

head: Plan
vCores
RAM
NVMe storage
Price/month (USD)
Confidence
rows: From the OVH US page. 500 Mbps bandwidth, unlimited traffic, daily backup of the previous 24 hours
Prices vary a lot between sources

items: One source says OVH has a 2026 VPS line with 6 configurations, from 4 vCores, 8 GB, 75 GB up to 24 vCores, 96 GB, 400 GB. Prices vary by region and currency.
Server location: one source says OVH has a Singapore data center for Asia. I haven't confirmed Sydney or Mumbai.
I haven't found a source confirming backup fees and terms for plans above VPS-1, so check on the order page.

sections.t: 2. What Hermes Agent needs

head: Source
Minimum
Recommended
rows: Same source, with the browser tool on
2 GB RAM or more, plus the --shm-size=1g option
Some posts say 2 GB RAM and 10 GB disk
Some posts recommend 2 cores, 8 GB RAM

items: Hermes calls models through external APIs, so the VPS doesn't need a GPU.
The 64K+ context model requirement only applies if you run the model yourself.
The hosting providers' 8 GB advice is far above the official level; I read it as cautious sales advice.

sections.t: 3. Which plan to pick (my pick)

head: Use case
Plan
Why
rows: Hermes with the Telegram gateway, no browser
Several times the official recommendation, cheapest
Hermes with the browser tool, scheduled runs, plus a few small bots
Spare RAM for the browser and Docker, a sensible step up
Several agents running in parallel, several browsers
Want to run an AI model on the VPS itself
These plans have no GPU, so call models through an API

sections.t: Bottom line: if you plan to use Hermes long term and want headroom, go with VPS-2. To save money, start with VPS-1 and upgrade when monitoring shows RAM is full. The biggest cost is usually the model API, not the VPS, so set a budget limit with your model provider from day one.
4. Checklist before buying

items.d: Run free -h and htop when the bot is busiest. If RAM is above roughly 70 to 80% or swap is used often, you need more RAM. If RAM is fine but CPU often hits 100%, you need more cores.

items.t: Decide whether you'll turn on the browser
items.d: If yes, plan for at least 2 GB for Hermes alone, plus RAM for your other bots.

items.t: Check plan, price and region on the OVH site
items.d: Look at the exact region and currency you're buying in, and check the backup terms.

items.t: Pick a location close to Vietnam
items.d: Prefer Singapore if the plan offers it.

sections.t: 5. Checklist for installing Hermes on the VPS
Take the exact install commands from the official Hermes docs (link at the end of this card). I don't copy them here to avoid version mismatches.

items.t: Create the VPS and basic security
items.d: Use a non-root user, log in with an SSH key, turn on the firewall. This is my general recommendation.
Follow the Hermes Docker docs.

items.t: Create a new Telegram bot for Hermes
items.d: Create it via @BotFather. One token should have only one program receiving messages (my general understanding, not checked in the Hermes docs). The LanhMar Contact Bot token is used by Apps Script for the website chat, so don't share it.

The docs describe: pull the nousresearch/hermes-agent image, run setup once, then run the gateway in the background with ~/.hermes mounted to /opt/data, port 8642, with --restart unless-stopped. If you turn on the browser, add --shm-size=1g.
Don't let two gateway containers share one data folder.

items.t: Add the Telegram token and model API key
items.d: Only put them in the config on the VPS, never in a repo or chat.

items.t: Set a budget limit with the model provider
items.d: Avoids an endless loop burning money.
Give the agent a few small tasks and check the logs before handing it real work.
This holds memory and config; lose it and you lose what the agent has learned.
After 1 to 2 weeks, check free -h again and upgrade if you're hitting the limit.

sections.t: 6. Security

items: The agent has broad permissions: run it on a separate VPS, away from important data, with minimal permissions.
Don't put ADMIN_KEY or the repo and Apps Script keys on this machine unless needed.
Content the agent reads (email, web) can hide malicious instructions. Don't let the agent follow everything it reads.
Read the Hermes project's security warnings carefully before granting broad permissions.

guide-ai-agent-ecosystem.title: The AI Agent ecosystem: Codex, Antigravity, Cursor, Copilot, OpenClaw, Hermes…
guide-ai-agent-ecosystem.note: Popular agents: Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, Cursor, Copilot, OpenClaw, Hermes… plus MCP, Skills and frameworks.

sections.t: This section helps you recognize the names you'll see in AI Agent docs before going deeper. The field moves very fast; info updated 24/10/2026, so open the original pages for the latest version.
Personal agents that run on your own machine or server

items.d: A personal agent running in the background on your machine, taking commands via WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack…; it can run commands, manage files, control a browser and automate tasks. Former names: Clawdbot, Moltbot; author Peter Steinberger. Note: its permissions are very broad, so run it in an isolated environment and grant access carefully.

A self-hosted agent that runs as a background process: persistent memory, writes its own skills from repeated tasks, many chat gateways (Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp…), scheduled runs, any model you like. Launched around February 2026. You still pay for the model and the server.

sections.t: Coding agents

items.d: An agent that reads and edits code and runs commands in your project folder; supports skills, hooks, MCP and subagents. Also available in IDEs and as a desktop app.
OpenAI's coding agent: runs as a CLI, in an IDE, or hands tasks to a cloud version to work on several in parallel so you can review the results.

A coding environment Google launched in late 2025 with the agent at its center: the agent plans, writes code, runs a browser to test, and leaves “artifacts” (plans, screenshots, recordings) for you to review. Uses Gemini and some other models.

A code editor built on VS Code with deep AI integration: chat, multi-file edits, an Agent mode that runs commands and fixes errors itself, plus background agents in the cloud. Lets you choose from many models.

Started as code suggestions, now has Agent mode in VS Code and a coding agent that takes GitHub issues, creates a branch, writes code and opens a pull request for you to review. Best fit if your team already uses GitHub.
Google's open-source command-line agent, in the same group as Claude Code and Codex CLI.
An IDE with an agent (Cascade) that understands the whole project, competing directly with Cursor.
An autonomous agent you assign work to like an engineer: it picks up tasks, writes code, tests it and sends back results.

sections.t: Standards and building blocks

items.d: An open standard for connecting agents to tools and data, like a “USB port” for AI. Anthropic announced it in late 2024, and many companies now support it.
A bundle of instructions plus scripts so an agent can redo a task the right way. It's an open standard, just donated to the Agentic AI Foundation (news from 22/10/2026 in AI News).

sections.t: General-purpose agents (no coding needed)

items.d: Turn on tools, browse the web, run code and read files right in the app you already use for multi-step work. The easiest place to start.
A cloud agent that takes a goal, then researches, writes reports, builds web pages and sends back the results on its own.

sections.t: AI automation with little or no code

items.d: Connect apps with drag-and-drop workflows and add AI steps. Good for “fixed workflow” level tasks, easy to control, beginner-friendly.

sections.t: Frameworks for developers

items.d: Build agents as state graphs, with control over flow and memory.
Organize several role-based agents to work together.
Microsoft's framework for agents to talk to and coordinate with each other.

sections.t: What to pick when starting out

items: Can't code yet and want to try first: use workflows (n8n, Zapier) or the tool modes in ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini.
Want your own assistant running 24/365: read the “Build a 24/365 assistant” doc, then try OpenClaw or Hermes on a separate machine with test data, not real data yet.
Can code: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot or Antigravity (combined with MCP and Skills), or a framework like LangGraph. Try one tool for a week before switching.

sections.t: For open-source agents with broad permissions like OpenClaw or Hermes: run them on a separate machine or server, away from important data, grant minimal permissions and read the project's security warnings carefully before use.

tool-facebook-cli.title: facebook-cli (fb): Facebook and Messenger for AI agents
tool-facebook-cli.note: A single-file Rust CLI that drives your Chrome already logged in to Facebook: read the feed, profiles, friends, search; read and send Messenger messages; post, comment, react, delete. Compact output for AI agents. MIT license.

sections.t: fb is a command-line tool for AI agents (and you) to use Facebook and Messenger. It drives a headless Chrome already logged in to your account and returns data as compact text lines to save tokens.
Repo info

head: Item
Details
rows: Rust (the page-control part is written in JavaScript)
0.1.5 (per Cargo.toml when I read it, latest commit 26/10/2026)
MIT (with an Apache 2.0 notice for part of the macOS key handling)
Google Chrome installed and logged in to Facebook in your everyday Chrome

sections.t: Highlights

items: A background process keeps the Chrome connection; each command runs in its own tab, so they can run in parallel (fb batch).
Chrome runs headless: no window, no stolen focus. The login session is copied once into fb's own Chrome profile.
Minimal output: tab-separated lines, no headers, 5-character reference codes (p3k9a, c8x2f…) reusable across all commands.
fb help is only about 450 tokens, good for AI agents to read quickly.
Recognizes the post, audience and delete buttons by their English, Vietnamese and French labels.

sections.t: Install (3 steps)
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hieu-lee/facebook-cli/main/install.sh | sh
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hieu-lee/facebook-cli/main/install.ps1 | iex

sections.cap: Log in once, then try it
sections.t:
fb login        # copy the Facebook session from your everyday Chrome, click Allow once
fb feed -n 3
fb help
My tip: before running a curl | sh style install command, open install.sh on GitHub and read through it once.
Main commands

head: Group
Command
What it does
rows: fb feed, posts, view, profile, friends, search, notifs
View the feed, posts from a person or page, comments, profiles, friends, search, notifications
fb chats, read, send, unsend, unlock
Chat list, read messages, send messages and files (up to 25MB), unsend messages, unlock end-to-end encrypted chats with a PIN
Post (with images, choose audience), comment, react, delete your own posts (to Trash)
fb batch, login, status, stop, quit, eval, shot, ax
Run several commands in parallel, manage sessions, run JS, take screenshots, view the accessibility tree
fb page NAME open, snapshot, click, fill, key, shot
Do anything on a named page (settings, group admin…) without dumping the whole DOM

sections.t: Config variables

head: Variable
Meaning
rows: Number of command tabs running at once (default 10, named pages max 6)
Auto-exit after this many idle seconds (default 900) and close Chrome
Chrome profile folder and state folder (default under ~/.cache/fb)
Use a Chrome you open yourself with a debugging port instead of the headless one

sections.t: Important notes before use

items: Facebook's terms restrict automated access. Only use it on your own account, at a human-like pace, and accept the risk of account restrictions. This is the repo README's own assessment.
Login cookies live in the ~/.cache/fb profile (or %LOCALAPPDATA%\fb on Windows). Anyone who can read this folder can use your session, so treat it like a password.
The headless Chrome is controlled via the DevTools protocol on a random 127.0.0.1 port with no authentication. Only use it on a personal machine, not a shared one.
Post, comment, send and delete commands are real actions on your account. With an AI agent, try read-only mode first and require confirmation before posting or sending.
Facebook's interface can change at any time, so the tool may need updates. The repo states clearly that not every feature is guaranteed to be tested.
End-to-end encrypted chats need your Messenger PIN: pass it via the FB_PIN variable or stdin, not as a command argument.

sections.t: Ideas for using it in the Library

items: Have an AI agent read and summarize messages, notifications and posts in the marketing groups you follow.
Draft posts with AI, then use fb post ... --to me to test-post as Only me before going public.
Pair with the AI Agent courses (Agent Boss, KesFlow) in the Library to build a fanpage management assistant.

edit-quay-co-ban.title: Filming basics: shot sizes, camera angles, lighting, gear
edit-quay-co-ban.note: Shot sizes, camera angles, the rule of thirds, 3-point lighting and reflectors, basic gear and a pre-shoot checklist.

sections.t: Sources: university video production guides and roundup articles on the web (see the end of this card). One is a 2008 checklist, so I only took the principles, not the old gear names. Most Vietnamese articles I found only covered gimbals and mics, so the angles and lighting parts come from English sources.
1. Shot sizes and camera angles
Cover all the shot sizes: wide shots for information, close shots for emotion. Also shoot B-roll and cutaways so you have something to insert when editing, especially for interviews.
2. Composition: the rule of thirds

Split the frame with 2 horizontal and 2 vertical lines and place the subject on a line or intersection. It's a guideline, not a hard rule, so break it when the shot needs it. Many cameras have a built-in grid to make this easy.
3. Lighting: 3-point lighting and reflectors

head: Light
Where to place it
What it does
rows: About 45 degrees in front of the subject
Opposite the key, about half its intensity
Separates the subject from the background

items: No fill light yet? Use a reflector or a white card instead, per the checklist.
Avoid strong light right behind the subject, as it easily turns them dark or into a silhouette.
Set white balance to match the light source, such as daylight or tungsten.

sections.t: 4. Basic gear

head: Gear
Notes
rows: Use one whenever you can; handheld is harder to keep steady than it feels
The minimum lighting kit per the checklists
Check audio levels before shooting. A directional mic picks up sound in front clearly and cuts surrounding noise. Use a windscreen outdoors
Stabilizes with motors and sensors, helps with tricky shots like POV and 360-degree rotation. Check phone compatibility and decide what you'll shoot before buying
Charged batteries, script or shot list
Prepare before getting to the location

sections.t: 5. Before you hit record

items.d: Check the light and noise.

items.t: Prepare a script or shot list
items.d: List the shot sizes and angles you need.
Test audio levels before shooting.

items.t: Set white balance and turn on the grid
items.d: Match the light source, turn on the rule-of-thirds grid.

items.t: Shoot extra B-roll and 20 seconds of room tone
items.d: Room tone helps you get cleaner audio in the edit.

tool-social-aio.title: Social AIO: a Chrome extension for managing social media
tool-social-aio.note: A toolbox in Chrome: download photos/videos, export comments, bulk-clean posts and friend lists, block seen receipts, lock pages with a password.

cta.title: Social AIO on the Chrome Web Store
cta.btn: Open on the Chrome Web Store

sections.t: The extension acts on the social media accounts you're logged in to. Bulk actions (deleting posts, unfriending, unfollowing…) are hard to undo and may break platform terms. Try on a few items first and review the permissions list when installing.
What it is

Social AIO (formerly FB AIO, Tools category on the Chrome Web Store, version 2.1, updated 31/7/2026) is a toolbox that bundles many social media management tasks into one extension. Per the store page, it has about 30,000 users and a 5.0 rating from about 2.8 thousand reviews. The developer states it isn't affiliated with any social media platform.
Main features (per the store page)

items.d: Download photos and videos; export a post's comments and reactions; save media from Instagram, Threads, TikTok; export your list of subscribed YouTube channels.
Change privacy, delete or archive many posts at once, with search and filters.
Review conversations, find the first message, download chats.
Track changes in your friend list, rank interaction levels, bulk unfriend, unfollow, unlike.
Block story seen and message read receipts, strip tracking parameters from links, lock some pages with a password stored on your machine.
Hide feed blocks, pause auto-refresh, track time spent on each website, add video controls on Facebook.

sections.t: How to use

items.d: Open the extension page on the Chrome Web Store, click Add to Chrome and read the requested permissions.

items.t: Log in to social media as usual
items.d: The extension works on the pages you have open, so log in to the account you want to manage first.
Try a task on a few items (one post, a few people) to see the result before doing it in bulk.
The store page links to the developer's support site (fbaio.org) and GitHub issues.

sections.t: Use it for the right things

items: Good for: backing up your own content, cleaning up a personal account, more privacy, tracking how much time you spend.
Be careful: bulk actions on accounts used for work, ads or fanpages. Going too fast can trigger the platform's anti-bot checks.
Don't use it to download or repost other people's content without permission.
The extension can read the social media pages you open: only install from the official store, keep an eye on updates and remove it if you no longer use it.

sections.t: The description and privacy commitments above are the developer's own words on the store page, not independently verified.

items: The three pieces of an AI coworker: Mindset (Instruction and Memory), Toolset (Connector, MCP), Skillset (Skills).
Session 2: a skill is the recipe, tools are the utensils. A skill is a folder with SKILL.md as the entry point, plus references and scripts when needed.

Session 3: Claude Cowork works directly on real files on your machine and runs several agents in parallel with Subagents. Three common mistakes when packaging a skill: no completion criteria, duplicated content, mixing human-facing docs into the skill.
Session 4: three ways AI looks up information (training data, web search, Deep Research) and using NotebookLM as an always-on knowledge base.
